Advances in development of tuberculosis vaccines and preventive drug therapies: current pipeline, evidence, and access.
abstract: Tuberculosis remains the leading cause of death from a single infectious agent globally. The WHO Global Tuberculosis Report 2025 indicates that progress towards the WHO End TB Strategy targets remains off track despite modest declines in incidence and mortality. In 2024, an estimated 10·7 million people developed tuberculosis and 1·23 million died from the disease. In this Series paper, we examine evidence published between Jan 6, 2020, and Jan 6, 2026, to provide an updated overview of tuberculosis vaccines and tuberculosis preventive treatment (TPT). As of June 4, 2026, 18 tuberculosis vaccine candidates are in active clinical development, including six in phase 3 (M72/AS01E, MTBVAC, VPM1002, GamTBvac, Immuvac [MIP], and BCG revaccination trials), representing the most diverse and advanced pipeline since the introduction of BCG in 1921. Platforms include live-attenuated mycobacterial vaccines (eg, MTBVAC), recombinant BCG-derived approaches (eg, VPM1002), protein-adjuvant subunit vaccines (eg, M72/AS01E), viral-vectored candidates (eg, AdHu5Ag85A, ChAdOx1.85A, and TB/FLU-04L), and inactivated whole-cell strategies (eg, DAR-901, RUTI, and Immuvac [MIP]). However, only a few candidates have progressed to late-stage efficacy evaluation. Short-course rifamycin-containing TPT regimens-1 month of daily isoniazid plus rifapentine, 3 months of once-weekly isoniazid plus rifapentine, 3 months of daily isoniazid plus rifampicin, and 4 months of daily rifampicin-show non-inferior efficacy and higher completion rates than 6-9 months of daily isoniazid monotherapy and are WHO-preferred options for drug-susceptible tuberculosis. In 2024, 5·3 million people at high risk of tuberculosis initiated TPT globally, including 3·5 million household contacts and 1·8 million people with HIV. For contacts of multidrug-resistant or rifampicin-resistant tuberculosis, randomised trials and pooled analyses support 6 months of daily levofloxacin to reduce incident multidrug-resistant tuberculosis. Bedaquiline-containing preventive regimens and shorter fluoroquinolone-based combinations are under clinical evaluation, but definitive phase 3 efficacy data are not yet available. The expansion of the vaccine pipeline alongside improved short-course preventive regimens offers a credible opportunity to accelerate tuberculosis incidence decline, although translation into population-level impact will depend on shown efficacy, sustained financing, reliable drug and vaccine supply, and effective implementation in high-burden settings.

title: State of the global tuberculosis epidemic: burden, progress towards WHO End TB Strategy targets and systemic challenges.
abstract: Mycobacterium tuberculosis remains the leading cause of death from a single infectious pathogen globally despite decades of effective chemotherapy. In 2024, an estimated 10·7 million people developed tuberculosis, including approximately 620 000 people living with HIV (PLHIV), and tuberculosis caused an estimated 1·23 million deaths overall, including approximately 150 000 deaths among PLHIV. Men accounted for more than half of the cases, and children represented a substantial burden, reflecting ongoing transmission and diagnostic gaps. Approximately a quarter of the world's population has been infected with M tuberculosis, with immunological evidence of previous or current infection. This population includes groups at increased risk of progression to tuberculosis disease, particularly those with recent infection, HIV, undernutrition, young age, or other clinical and social vulnerabilities. Following 3 years of COVID-19-related setbacks, global tuberculosis incidence declined modestly (1%) from 2023 to 2024 but remains higher than in 2020 and far off-track to meet the 2025 WHO End TB Strategy milestones. Case detection improved to 8·3 million notifications (78% of estimated incident cases), supported by expanded molecular diagnostics; however, prevalence surveys continue to reveal substantial proportions of bacteriologically confirmed but asymptomatic tuberculosis, highlighting persistent transmission and missed diagnoses. 30 high-burden countries accounted for 87% of cases, led by India, Indonesia, the Philippines, China, Pakistan, Nigeria, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and Bangladesh. M tuberculosis-HIV co-infection remains a major driver of mortality in sub-Saharan Africa. Drug-resistant tuberculosis threatens progress: of 390 000 estimated multidrug-resistant or rifampicin-resistant tuberculosis cases in 2024, only 42% initiated treatment, although treatment success improved to 71%. Tuberculosis-preventive treatment reached 5·3 million people, including 58% of PLHIV and 25% of eligible household contacts, well below global targets. Persistent undernutrition, poverty, HIV, diabetes, smoking, alcohol use, air pollution, migration, and conflict continue to shape tuberculosis epidemiology. With financing at only 27% of global targets, accelerated prevention, proactive case finding, social protection, and sustained political commitment are essential to eliminate tuberculosis.

title: Extraperitoneal Single-Port Robotic-Assisted Radical Cystectomy with Orthotopic Ne-obladder: Technique and Surgical Considerations.
abstract:
Introduction

Radical cystectomy (RC) is the standard therapy for muscle-invasive bladder cancer (MIBC) and refractory high-risk non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer (1-3). Single-port robot-assisted radical cystectomy (RARC) offers notable minimally invasive advantages (4-6), whereas conventional transperitoneal approaches are associated with intestinal and gastrointestinal complications (7). This study evaluated an optimized extraperitoneal single-port RARC with orthotopic neobladder reconstruction for improved surgical safety and clinical outcomes.

Materials and methods

A 57-year-old male presented with three months of intermittent painless gross hematuria. Pelvic CT revealed a bladder mass. Preoperative biopsy confirmed high-grade urothelial carcinoma with muscularis propria invasion, and the patient received gemcitabine-cisplatin neoadjuvant chemotherapy before radical surgery. Preoperative MRI identified a 3.2×2.9×2.6 cm bladder lesion without extravesical invasion or lymphadenopathy. During the procedure, the patient was placed in a supine position with buttocks elevated. A 5-cm infraumbilical single incision was made for da Vinci Xi-assisted extraperitoneal RARC, and a single-port multichannel device was deployed through the incision. Robotic instruments including a 30° endoscope, monopolar scissors, bipolar forceps, and a robotic stapler were arranged in a chopstick configuration. Via the extraperitoneal approach, we mobilized the bilateral ureters, bilateral vas deferens, and umbilical artery, dissected the bladder lateral ligaments with vascular ligation, and established a sufficient extraperitoneal working space. Bladder and prostate dissection was performed along the perivesical avascular plane, with careful protection and precise hemostasis of the dorsal venous complex. Standard pelvic lymphadenectomy was concurrently conducted during radical resection of the bladder and prostate (8). A segment of ileum was then harvested to construct an orthotopic neobladder (9), followed by anastomosis with the bilateral ureters and urethral stump.

Results

Operative time was 400 minutes with 200 mL blood loss and no transfusion. No perioperative complications occurred, and the patient was discharged on postoperative day 6. Pathological diagnosis was pT2aN0M0 with negative surgical margins and negative lymph nodes. The 12-month follow-up showed no tumor recurrence, normal renal function, complete daytime continence, and mild nocturnal incontinence requiring one nightly pad.

Conclusions

Extraperitoneal single-port RARC with orthotopic neobladder reconstruction is a feasible minimally invasive procedure for MIBC. The optimized infraumbilical single-incision technique preserves peritoneal integrity and avoids intestinal mobilization, effectively reducing abdominal complications. It achieves reliable oncological results and improves patients' postoperative continence and quality of life.

title: Robot-Assisted Partial Nephrectomy in a High-Complexity Renal Tumor in a Horseshoe Kidney.
abstract:
Introduction

Horseshoe kidney is an uncommon congenital fusion anomaly that can make renal tumor surgery especially challenging because of altered rotation, limited mobility, variable vascular supply, and an unpredictable collecting system (1-7). This video presents a robot-assisted partial nephrectomy for a high-complexity renal tumor in this setting.

Case presentation

A 33-year-old man, with ECOG 0 and no relevant comorbidities, was diagnosed with a 7.5-cm solid renal mass in the central posterior portion of the left moiety of a horseshoe kidney. The lesion had a RENAL score of 10p. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography and three-dimensional reconstruction were used to understand the relationship between the tumor, aberrant vessels, renal hilum, and collecting system, supporting the decision to attempt nephron-sparing surgery (5, 8). Surgical technique and results: The procedure was performed through a transperitoneal robotic approach with the patient in right lateral decubitus using the Da Vinci Si platform. Port placement followed a standard renal robotic configuration, with a paramedian supraumbilical camera port, three robotic working ports along a craniocaudal lateral axis, a caudal fourth-arm port, and two medial assistant ports for suction, exposure, and support during renorrhaphy. After exposure of the horseshoe kidney and left hilar dissection, two arterial branches and one renal vein were identified. Tumor excision was performed under vascular control, with 20 minutes of warm ischemia and no collecting system opening, followed by two-layer absorbable renorrhaphy with adjunctive hemostatic agents. The operative time was 150 minutes. No transfusion, conversion, drain placement, or relevant immediate complication occurred. The urinary catheter was removed after 24 hours, and the patient was discharged 72 hours after surgery. Pathology showed clear cell renal cell carcinoma, Fuhrman grade 3, pT2N0M0, with negative surgical margins. During 12 months of oncologic follow-up, renal function remained stable and semiannual imaging showed no evidence of recurrence. Contemporary video reports have also emphasized the feasibility of advanced robotic renal surgery and complex partial nephrectomy strategies in selected patients (9, 10).

Conclusion

In a carefully selected patient, robot-assisted partial nephrectomy supported by three-dimensional planning was feasible for a complex renal tumor in a horseshoe kidney, with negative surgical margins, preserved renal function, and no recurrence during 12 months of follow-up.

Building competency in navigation bronchoscopy: Development and evaluation of a structured training programme.
abstract:
Background

Cone-beam CT-guided navigation bronchoscopy (CBCT-NB) is a minimally invasive technique for diagnosing pulmonary nodules combining endoscopic navigation with real-time 3D imaging. The procedure requires advanced bronchoscopic skills and interpretation of multiple imaging modalities. Despite evidence that simulation-based education enhances procedural safety and performance, no standardised training programmes for CBCT-NB have yet been established. This study describes the development and evaluation of a structured training programme for pulmonologists new to CBCT-NB.

Methods

A multidisciplinary expert panel developed a stepwise CBCT-NB training programme comprising online theoretical e-learning, live case observation at an expert centre, a structured one-day hands-on simulation session, and on-site supervision during the initial clinical procedures. Pulmonologists from Dutch hospitals preparing to implement CBCT-NB were enrolled. Participants' expectations, perceived learning needs, and post-training experiences were explored through semi-structured interviews and analysed using thematic analysis.

Results

Nine pulmonologists from five hospitals participated. Participants expressed a strong need for structured, practical instructions, particularly regarding procedural workflow, multimodal image interpretation, equipment handling, and use of augmented fluoroscopy software. Following completion of the programme, all reported increased self-confidence and improved perceived competency. Hands-on simulation was consistently identified as a key component for developing technical and cognitive skills and was considered essential preparation before independent clinical practice.

Conclusion

The structured multimodal CBCT-NB training programme facilitates confidence and addresses learner-identified competency needs among novice navigation bronchoscopists. The findings offer practical guidance for the structured implementation and training of novel medical technological interventions. Future research should evaluate long-term skill retention, objective competency outcomes, and clinical effectiveness.

Robot-Assisted Radical Prostatectomy in a Post-Enucleation Gland.
abstract:
Purpose

Holmium laser enucleation of the prostate (HoLEP) is an established treatment for benign prostatic obstruction, and some patients subsequently prove to have prostate cancer (1-3). Enucleation leaves fibrosis that displaces the anatomical landmarks relevant to radical prostatectomy (4, 5). We present a robot-assisted radical prostatectomy (RARP) performed after HoLEP.

Materials and methods

A 64-year-old man underwent HoLEP; biopsy subsequently showed adenocarcinoma of the right lobe, ISUP grade 3. PSA was 0.51 ng/mL; MRI demonstrated a 0.4 cm PI-RADS 4 lesion at the right mid-base. RARP was performed 29 months later on a da Vinci Xi system. Without the adenoma, the capsule is flaccid and offers no counter-resistance; without haptic feedback, the planes of the bladder neck (6) and neurovascular bundle (7) become indistinct. A wide bladder neck may admit the balloon into the fossa; overinflating it to 40 mL or tracing extravesical landmarks restores the anatomical reference. Retzius-sparing and transvesical approaches are recognized alternatives (8, 9). The video demonstrates a thickened Denonvilliers fascia and the use of the 30-degree lens rotated 180 degrees to open the posterior plane.

Results

Six ports were used (four robotic, two assistant); console time was 90 minutes with an estimated blood loss of 75 mL. Nerve-sparing was bilateral, and bladder neck reconstruction was not required. The patient was discharged on postoperative day 1; the catheter was removed on day 5. Pathology revealed adenocarcinoma of both lobes, Gleason 7 (4+3), pT2c, with negative surgical margins. At six weeks, the patient was continent without pads and had an undetectable PSA.

Conclusions

RARP after HoLEP is feasible. To our knowledge, this is the first video article dedicated to this operation, demonstrating each post-enucleation anatomical obstacle and a practical surgical response. The bladder neck and posterior plane warrant particular caution.

title: Robotic Totally Intracorporeal Bilateral Boari Flap Reconstruction for Complex Bilateral Ureteral Strictures: A Step-by-Step Technique.
abstract:
Purpose

Boari flap reconstruction is effective for unilateral ureteral strictures (1-5), but its use for bilateral disease is rarely reported. Robotic surgery offers enhanced visualization and dexterity for complex ureteral reconstruction (4, 6-9). We describe robotic totally intracorporeal bilateral Boari flap (BBF) reconstruction for bilateral mid- and distal ureteral strictures (BMDUS).

Materials and methods

A 42-year-old woman with BMDUS underwent BBF reconstruction. The left ureter was dissected, ligated, and transected proximal to the stricture, then trimmed to healthy tissue until a 10-Fr catheter passed smoothly; the same steps were repeated on the right. After measuring each ureteral defect, bilateral inverted U-shaped bladder flaps were tailored and hitched to the ipsilateral psoas tendons. A double-J stent was placed in each ureter. The healthy proximal ureters were anastomosed to the corresponding flaps, and both flaps were tubularized with running sutures. The bladder was then closed and a drain was placed.

Results

The procedure was completed successfully without conversion to open surgery. Operative time was 263 minutes, estimated blood loss was 55 mL, and bilateral 6-cm Boari flaps were created. The urinary catheter, double-J stents, and nephrostomy tubes were removed at 7 days, 5 weeks, and 6 weeks, respectively. At 12 months, bladder capacity was 352 mL, post-void residual volume was 8 mL, maximum flow rate was 26 mL/s, and eGFR had increased from 36.0 to 50.6 mL/min/1.73 m². At 35 months, the patient remained symptom-free with no late complications.

Conclusions

Robotic totally intracorporeal BBF reconstruction is technically feasible. Larger studies with long-term follow-up are warranted. Funding This research received funding support from the National Natural Science Foundation of China (82470724) and Zhongnan Hospital of Wuhan University (grant no. rcyj20230102 to Bing Li).

title: Radiopharmaceuticals for Melanoma Theranostics.
abstract: Malignant melanoma (MM) remains a formidable clinical challenge due to its high metastatic potential and the eventual emergence of resistance to current BRAF/MEK and immune checkpoint inhibitors. To address these limitations, the theranostic strategy integrating diagnostic imaging with targeted radionuclide therapy to enable personalized treatment has gained significant traction. Current research primarily exploits the overexpression of the melanocortin 1 receptor (MC1R), very late antigen-4 (VLA-4), and melanin as primary molecular targets for radiopharmaceutical development. For MC1R, α-MSH peptide analogs have been engineered with β-emitters such as <sup>177</sup>Lu and <sup>90</sup>Y for peptide receptor radionuclide therapy (PRRT), as well as α-emitters like <sup>225</sup>Ac and <sup>212</sup>Pb (β<sup>- </sup>decay to <sup>212</sup>Bi and then emit α particles) for targeted alpha therapy (TAT), showing high specificity and rapid clearance. Concurrently, VLA-4-targeted platforms utilizing high-affinity LLP2A ligands have been optimized through PEGylation and albumin-binding strategies to enhance bioavailability and tumor retention. Beyond these primary receptors, this review evaluates alternative strategies, including copper transporter (CTR1) targeting with <sup>64</sup>CuCl<sub>2</sub> and the use of gold nanocages for multimodal applications. Together, these advancements represent a critical shift toward image-guided, dosimetry-driven radionuclide therapies that may work synergistically with existing immunotherapies to improve survival in metastatic melanoma.

title: Registration accuracy, time, and osteotomy outcomes across four strategies for task-autonomous robotic maxillofacial osteotomy.
abstract:
Objectives

To compare four registration strategies for task-autonomous robotic maxillofacial osteotomy.

Methods

A maxillofacial model was constructed from imaging data. The maxilla and mandible were registered separately using splint-based landmark registration (SL), dental-landmark registration (DL), dental-surface registration (DS), and bone-surface registration (BS). The target-registration error (TRE) was measured in three osteotomy regions, and registration time was recorded. Osteotomies were then performed using a task-autonomous robotic system. The actual and planned osteotomy surfaces were compared using the root mean square (RMS) deviation, mean signed deviation, and angular deviation.

Results

All four strategies achieved mean TREs of less than 0.8 mm. In the Le Fort I region, TRE was lower for BS than for SL (0.398 ± 0.126 vs. 0.580 ± 0.098 mm; P = 0.0045). Mandibular TREs showed a significant strategy-by-region interaction (P = 0.0031); in the genioplasty region, DS and BS yielded lower TREs than SL and DL. In the mandibular angle region, DS yielded lower TREs than SL and DL, and BS yielded lower TREs than DL. SL had the shortest registration time for both jaws. In the genioplasty region, DL resulted in greater RMS and angular deviations than the other strategies, whereas in the mandibular angle region, DS resulted in lower angular deviation than SL and DL.

Conclusions

Registration strategy significantly influenced TRE, registration time, and mandibular osteotomy accuracy outcomes. All four strategies achieved submillimetric TREs. Overall, surface-based registration (BS and DS) yielded TREs that were lower than or comparable to those of landmark-based registration (SL and DL) and showed favorable performance for selected mandibular osteotomy accuracy outcomes. However, no consistent difference in accuracy was identified between DS and BS.

Clinical significance

Surface-based registration may support accurate robot-assisted osteotomy when adequate dentition or bony surfaces are accessible.

title: Comparable clinical outcomes but different postoperative Dynamic Alignment of the Knee (DyAK) patterns between cruciate-retaining and posterior-stabilized inserts in functionally aligned robotic-assisted total knee arthroplasty.
abstract:
Purpose

The influence of polyethylene insert design during robotic-assisted total knee arthroplasty (TKA) performed according to functional alignment (FA) principles remains poorly understood. This study compared cruciate-retaining (CR) and posterior-stabilized (PS) inserts with respect to implant positioning, clinical outcomes, implant survivorship and postoperative dynamic knee behaviour using the Dynamic Alignment of the Knee (DyAK) classification.

Methods

A retrospective comparative study was performed on 284 primary functionally aligned robotic-assisted TKAs. The cohort comprised 148 CR and 136 PS fixed-bearing cemented implants with a minimum follow-up of 3 years (median 44.5 months). Clinical outcomes included Knee Society Score (KSS) and Forgotten Joint Score (FJS). Intraoperative robotic implant positioning, bone resections, polyethylene thickness, DyAK classification, complications and Kaplan-Meier implant survivorship were compared between groups.

Results

The CR group demonstrated greater preoperative varus alignment (median robotic hip-knee-ankle angle [rHKA] 5° vs. 3°, p = 0.01). Compared with PS implants, CR inserts were implanted with greater tibial varus (2° vs. 1°, p < 0.0001), greater posterior tibial slope (3° vs. 1°, p < 0.0001) and slightly greater femoral external rotation (p = 0.009). Polyethylene inserts >9 mm were required more frequently in the PS group (39.0% vs. 15.5%, p < 0.0001). At final follow-up, KSS knee (p = 0.56), KSS function (p = 0.62) and FJS (p = 0.06) were comparable between groups. No statistically significant difference in survivorship was detected for aseptic loosening (0.68% vs. 0.74%, p = 0.95) and all-cause revision (2.03% vs. 1.47%, p = 0.72). The DyAK classification changed significantly more frequently in the PS group than in the CR group (69.9% vs. 52.7%, p = 0.003), despite similar postoperative clinical outcomes.

Conclusion

CR and PS polyethylene inserts showed no significant differences in final clinical scores or implant survivorship at a minimum follow-up of 3 years but demonstrated different patterns of postoperative dynamic alignment, suggesting that the DyAK classification may provide complementary information beyond conventional outcome measures.

Level of evidence

Level III.

title: 中文書名:微流體環境中的智能機器人定位極限 MICROFLUIDIC ENVIRONMENT IN INTELLIGENT ROBOT LOCALIZATION AT THE LIMIT This 777-page English research monograph asks whether intelligent robot localization in microfluidic environments can improve sample-identity probability without increasing contact impulse or carryover. The book contains 30 mathematical research plates, 82 chapters, 410 single-page studies, 200 Research Gates and 33 Phoenix Answer Embryos. It covers microfluidic flow, optical and multimodal localization, state estimation, data association, closed-loop control, sample identity, uncertainty, blinded fault tests and independent reconstruction. The work is nonclinical and hypothesis-generating. It does not claim completed clinical testing, proven in-body efficacy or autonomous medical authority. Label-free Raman spectroscopy for cancer therapy response: from methodological framework to clinical translation.
abstract: The early detection of therapy-induced biomolecular changes and the prediction of therapeutic response remain major challenges in oncology. Current clinical methods often assess treatment response through macroscopic or morphological endpoints, whereas molecular alterations associated with sensitivity, resistance, or recurrence may arise earlier and remain undetected. Raman spectroscopy offers a label-free and non-destructive approach to probe the intrinsic biochemical composition of cells, tissues, and biofluids, providing spectral and spatial information that can support therapy response prediction and longitudinal monitoring. This review discusses Raman-based technologies for cancer therapy assessment, from preclinical models to emerging clinical applications. We first outline the clinical need for rapid, non-destructive, and molecularly informative tools, considering tumor heterogeneity, therapy resistance, the tumor microenvironment, and current standards for response evaluation. We then provide a methodological framework for selecting Raman modalities, including spontaneous Raman (SR) spectroscopy, surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (SERS), stimulated Raman spectroscopy (SRS), and coherent anti-Stokes Raman spectroscopy (CARS), together with key considerations on acquisition strategies, multimodal integration, experimental design, preprocessing, feature analysis, and machine learning. We summarize Raman spectral biomarkers associated with therapy-induced changes in nucleic acids, proteins, lipids, metabolites, extracellular matrix components, and anticancer drugs, and critically examine studies using Raman spectroscopy to predict or monitor responses to major therapeutic approaches. Finally, we discuss barriers to clinical translation, including acquisition speed, inter-instrument reproducibility, preclinical model limitations, regulatory requirements, workflow integration, clinical trials, and prospective validation. Overall, Raman spectroscopy emerges as a promising platform for molecular phenotyping in precision oncology, provided that future studies progress toward standardized, clinically validated, and actionable workflows.

Robotic Assessment of Thumb Proprioception after Stroke: Reliability, Validity, and Sensitivity.
abstract:
Objective

Despite the thumb's critical role in dexterity and its dense sensory innervation, thumb proprioceptive deficits after stroke remain limited due to the limited nature of clinical assessments. This study evaluated the reliability, validity, and sensitivity of a novel robotic assessment of thumb proprioception, SomatoCircleJump (SCJ), in individuals with chronic stroke.

Design

Cross-sectional psychometric study evaluating the reliability, validity and sensitivity of SCJ using baseline data from a clinical trial, with assessments conducted twice 5-10 days apart. In SCJ, a robot moved the visually occluded thumb, and participants indicated when the thumb passed a visual target.

Setting

University-based rehabilitation research laboratory.

Participants

Thirty-five stroke survivors with residual unilateral hand weakness and 24 healthy age-matched controls.

Interventions

Not applicable.

Main outcome measures

SCJ proprioceptive error, defined as the angular difference between actual thumb position and the visually presented target. Test-retest reliability was assessed with Intraclass Correlation Coefficient (ICC). Validity and sensitivity were evaluated by comparing SCJ with the Fugl-Meyer Assessment Sensory Scale for the upper extremity (FMA-S) thumb position item, and two robotic proprioception tests, one for the thumb (ThumbSense) and one for the fingers (Crisscross).

Results

SCJ demonstrated good test-retest reliability (ICC = 0.82, 95% CI [0.72-0.87]). SCJ error correlated significantly with FMA-S (ρ = -0.56, p < 0.001), ThumbSense accuracy (ρ = -0.62, p < 0.001), and Crisscross error (ρ = 0.61, p < 0.001). Using a 2SD criterion relative to controls, SCJ identified thumb proprioceptive impairment in 61% of stroke participants, compared with 23% identified by FMA-S.

Conclusions

SCJ is a reliable, valid, and sensitive assessment of dynamic thumb proprioception after stroke. It revealed that thumb proprioceptive deficits are common and related to finger proprioception deficits, supporting its use in future studies of sensory impairment and rehabilitation outcomes.
